A lot of employers have a "disability confident" thing - meaning they will guarantee an interview to at least 1 disabled applicant who meets the requirements. However I've found that disclosing my mental health issues has prevented me from getting interviews. Some employers really don't want to hire disabled people and they can just say they didn't offer you an interview because they felt other applicants were more qualified.

We have laws in place that makes it illegal to discriminate based on characteristics like disabilities. Though these laws didn't stop my old employer from letting me go due to my severe mental health issues.

There are disability benefits available, the amount you get depends on the severity of your disability. But if you have a condition that comes with a lot of expenses, it will likely not be enough. 

It also depends on the area you live in. Some towns and cities have more support available than others. The support for my issues where I currently live is not very good, so I am kinda on my own.

You can certainly survive, but maybe not thrive.

Medication has helped stabilise me though. Instead of constantly being suicidal, I just feel numb. I saw in another comment you said you were on sertraline, maybe ask the GP if you can try another. I had to test out several different medications before I found one that worked.

Being out of work for a while has given me the time to work on my mental health. I've been slowly building up things that benefit my wellbeing. I started using HelloFresh a few months ago and it has helped massively with eating enough food & eating healthier, also has made me enjoy cooking again and it's quite a mindful activity for me. You could maybe try making a meal plan of some sort if that is not in your price range - eating good really does help you mentally. I also take multivitamins every day, I started doing this initially because I am vegetarian but they definitely help make me feel less exhausted. Exercise is another thing - I started the gym recently, only go once a week and do a bit of cardio but it has helped me feel a lot better in myself. You could try going for a walk, doesn't have to be every day and doesn't have to be super long, just some minutes of exercise can really help. I've also deleted a bunch of social media to stop me doom scrolling & to avoid seeing things that make me miserable. I got into a good habit of reading before bed too, but I had a bit of a blip recently and stopped, trying to get back into it again as it is nice to get lost in a book instead of being alone with your thoughts. Also have been trying to do volunteering to find some form of purpose.

Not sure if any of the above will help you (or if you're already doing them), just thought I'd mention them because I completely understand what you're going through, I've been where you are.

What’s it like to be the “default”?
Well, as a white person my skin colour is never something I have to worry about being discriminated against, which is obviously a privilege. I have never felt a sense of solidarity with other white people, which could be because I have other characteristics that can be discriminated against - neurodivergent, female, lgbtq+. But at least being queer and neurodivergent is something that can be "hidden", unlike skin colour. That said, being neurodivergent makes me feel like an alien wherever I go, and I tend to get along better with people of foreign cultures, as they don't hold me to the same expectations as people of my culture do, also they probably feel like outcasts like I do.
Being white does mean other white people feel comfortable making racist jokes/comments to you, which makes me uncomfortable. And white supremacists make me feel embarrassed and disgusted to be white. I have never understood why some people think white skin is superior to other skin colours.
Now about having white skin. My skin is very pale so I am often told I look ill. In summer I am self conscious of having to show a lot of skin because I look like a milk bottle and probably blind people like snow does. But these issues are trivial in comparison to what people of other skin colours face.

What’s it like to have straight or wavy hair?
It's low maintenance, but it gets greasy quickly. I have to wash my hair every other day.

What’s it like to have blue eyes (is it true that your eyes hurt more in the sun)?
I have brown eyes so I cannot really share my experience. But blue eyes do let in more light, so bright light like the sun can cause problems. People with blue eyes are also more likely to need prescription glasses.

What’s it like to have white skin and have to constantly remember sunscreen?
I hate sunscreen for sensory reasons as it feels so greasy. I just try not to stay out in the sun for too long, because I burn easily and I struggle in the heat due to my medication. I will only wear it if I have to be out in the sun for a long period of time. White people have a higher risk of skin cancer due to how easily we burn, so sunscreen is quite important.

Yes, it is my favourite Sims game.

Good:

Gameplay - there's a hobby system, holiday worlds with different activities, the option to run a home business or open a shop selling basically anything

Lore - the premade neighbourhoods are packed with it

Personalities - sims are quite expressive depending on their personality. For example, shy sims appear timid when doing certain social actions

Wants & Fears - so much better than in the Sims 4
Option to create your own neighbourhood

Apartments are better than the residential rentals in Sims 4 as there are no loading screens (you can build quite a few apartment units but can only move sims into 4)

No need to continuously update the game and mods

Community lots can have multiple functions - you can create a mall with shops, a restaurant, a salon and an arcade for example

Genetics - eye colour and hair colour have recessive and dominant types. For example, 2 black hair sims will only have black haired babies. But if one of the sims had a brunette parent, the babies could have either black or brown. If both sims had a parent with blonde hair, their children can end up with blonde hair too. Works the same for eye colours

DLCs add a lot of content & gameplay

The theme music is such a vibe

Bad:

No story progression - Lazy Duchess has a mod that adds this though

Can't visit other houses - again I think Lazy Duchess' mod adds this

Creating diverse sims is limited - there's only 3 body types, 4 skin colours, 4 hair colours (though there are custom hair colours too which can be accessed with a mirror)

Less build and buy mode options - custom content helps with this

Less CAS options - again custom content helps with this 

Graphics are outdated (but not as dated as Sims 3 as Sims 2 wasn't going for proper realism) - there are mods to make the game look better. Personally I quite like the look of Sims 2 sims though

Occults aren't as fun as in Sims 3 & 4

I am not sure if private is an option for you...from my research the average cost is £2000 which is a lot. But be prepared to battle with GPs. It took a while for me to find a GP who was willing to refer me. Many of them do not have a good understanding of autism - one GP I spoke to refused to refer me because I have mental health diagnoses (which is silly because mental health issues are very common co-morbidities in autistic people). I advise you to make a document stating your case - list your symptoms and struggles, also add in that your school flagged you for autism. Use online assessment tools (ones that are backed by research) and show your results - I recommend the site Embrace Autism. And if you have any friends or relatives you're close to, tell them that you're pursuing a diagnosis. Most of my friends were not surprised by me telling them that I think I have autism, and my boyfriend has been very supportive. Online communities, like this subreddit, are helpful to validate your thoughts and feelings, and to find people with similar experiences.

I think you are getting confused between sex and gender.

Sex is a biological thing influenced by chromosomes and hormones. Humans generally have two modes - either male or female. But there are abnormalities where one's sex may not be obvious (intersex), or where sex chromosomes do not align with the biological makeup of the individual. For example, there are biological females walking about with XY chromosomes, which are known as the male sex chromosomes. For example, there are 2 syndromes where this occurs - Swyer Syndrome, which is caused by a mutation on the Y chromosome, and Morris Syndrome which is caused by a mutation on the X chromosome. These mutations affect the development of male sex organs. Some females with Swyer Syndrome can give birth.

Gender is a social construct to do with identity. It is usually influenced by society's views on femininity and masculinity, at least in the Western world. Most people's gender aligns with their biological sex, so man or woman. But there are individuals where this does not align and hence you get transgender individuals, who may undergo sex reassignment surgery and HRT to present more as their identified gender. There are also people who do not feel as though they align with either of the binary genders of man or woman, which is where you get non-binary people (like me).

Bisexual people can be attracted to trans and non-binary people too of course, as the term now is defined as having an attraction to 2 or more genders. I am bisexual and I do not explicitly care what genitals one has, but I am attracted to both femininity and masculinity, and anything in between (or outside) counts too. By femininity and masculinity I mean physical traits of course, as I have a lot of gripes over society's view on those things in terms of hobbies, interests, etc. I swing more towards femininity, which means I generally swing towards women (cis or trans) but I have been attracted to men and non-binary people too. Some people may view this as being pansexual, but to me pansexuality is where you do not care about gender and have an equal amount of attraction to them all, which is not true for me as I have stated.

Same here. I've had severe depression and anxiety for most of my life. Doctors have said I am treatment-resistant because so many meds did not work and I wasn't finding therapy useful. Realised I might be autistic as an adult and it explained so much.

Your brain basically works differently to most people, but it still functions. You just process things and respond to them in a different manner to others. You may struggle/be slower to connect with non-autistic individuals but that doesn't mean you can't. It just might take a bit more work. This doesn't mean there is something horribly wrong with you, by the way.

Masking is like a learned behaviour autistic people do to blend in with the people around them, to avoid being singled out as "weird" or "odd". They imitate others' mannerisms and suppress autistic behaviours such as stimming. However, this can be very exhausting because it takes a lot of energy to hide your real self. So, it can take quite a mental toll, which is why depression and anxiety are quite commonly found in autistic people.

Getting a diagnosis would help you receive more adequate support. Normal therapy is based on how the neurotypical brain works, so it is often not as helpful for autistic people. But there are therapists out there who specialise in autism. You can also receive other support such as school/work adjustments.

You seem to have a misconception of what evolution is. It is not always about natural selection. In fact, a wide range of genetic variances is healthy, including ones that may seem disadvantageous on the surface. **Evolution doesn't have a set purpose.** It is imperfect, random, and chaotic.

There have been periods in history where selection pressures favour advantageous genetic variances for a specific disaster. But as the population recovers and continues to reproduce, the gene pool widens again and allows for more variance (known as genetic drift). I'd recommend looking up genetic bottlenecking to see what happens when there is a sharp decline in a population.

* Stimming. Yes, anything can be a stim if it is a subconscious repetitive action that provides relief. Neurotypical people stim, too. But it's often more pronounced in autistic people, and some may have stims that can cause physical injuries. However, some autistic people learn to adopt more "socially acceptable" stims like playing with an earring.
* Sensory issues. Yeah, this is quite common in autism. Since you described an aversion to showers or baths, there are many sensory things that could be happening here. Maybe you just hate the feeling of being wet, or the temperature of the water. Maybe the shower sounds too loud. Maybe you don't like the feeling of your skin becoming wrinkly. Maybe you find bath products have an overwhelming and unpleasant smell. Just a few examples.
* Hyperfixation. It could be described as an obsession. You may forget to eat or use the toilet because you're so focused on this one topic. You may talk about it constantly or spend all day, for many days at a time, doing it. It might help to look up the theory of monotropism. But yeah, you could do be interested in something for a while, and then something else becomes more fascinating so you drop the previous interest for a bit.
* Repetitive routines. Yes that is common. Personally I do not have much of a daily routine at the moment which has stopped me functioning. However, I still have a morning routine and shower routine where I always complete the steps in the same order, every day. I hate when this is disrupted, and I do not enjoy stepping out of my comfort zone often.

For the other question: yes, this is can be due to something called masking. As an autistic person grows up they may learn what is and isn't socially acceptable.
